criteria.name: Introduction — Identifies ethical issues and broad links to engineering design; discusses the context of ethical issues in engineering organisations; identifies relevant stakeholders when considering the ethical issues.
criteria.reasoning: Three distinct ethical issues (calendar-driven test coverage, data loss misclassified as harmless, conflict of interest) are named and tied to engineering design and organisational decision rights. Table 1 gives six stakeholder groups with interests and decision authority, including patients who cannot consent.

evidence.quote: First, test coverage is being set by the release calendar instead of by risk, which is a design-process decision made by the organisation
Table 1: Stakeholders, their interests and the decision each controls.

criteria.name: Balanced Discussion — Discusses objective arguments for and against decisions on the ethical issues; draws a conclusion on how stakeholders should make decisions about the issues.
criteria.reasoning: Each pro-shipping argument is stated fairly then rebutted on its own terms, which is genuine objectivity rather than one-sided advocacy. Table 2 assigns the risk carrier per option, and conclusions are drawn separately for Rachel, management, the health department and the chip supplier.

evidence.quote: These arguments are sound for ordinary customers, but each one weakens for this contract.
Rachel should withhold quality sign-off for the health contract, record the untested failure modes in writing and escalate to management.

criteria.name: Compelling Argument that supports conclusion — The report forms a compelling argument that justifies the conclusion; the body follows a logical structure, with linked paragraphs and content ordered to support the argument; arguments demonstrate a systematic understanding of the ethical issues for all stakeholders.
criteria.reasoning: Structure carries the argument: issues to stakeholder map, then for/against, then a decision rule, then option comparison, then recommendation. The conclusion restates the measured-reduced-accepted criterion established in the body, so it is fully supported rather than tacked on.

evidence.quote: Options B and C respect every stakeholder's interests better than either extreme.
The ethical course is to ship only when the risk has been measured, reduced where practical and accepted by an informed customer.

criteria.name: Research and Evidence — Arguments are substantiated with adequate references and qualitative/quantitative evidence; research demonstrates a balanced, in-depth understanding of the topic.
criteria.reasoning: Eight relevant sources including a primary standards document, a professional code and four well-chosen external cases. Quantitative evidence ($475m, $4.3bn, 19,000 appointments, six Therac-25 patients) is paired with qualitative Code of Ethics reasoning. Counter-evidence is acknowledged where the WannaCry analogy is imperfect.

evidence.quote: at least 81 of 236 hospital trusts in England were disrupted, an estimated 19,000 appointments were cancelled
Intel had to offer replacements and took a charge of US$475 million

criteria.name: Report Structure, Format and Language — The report includes appropriate sections serving their functions (abstract, introduction, body, and conclusion); maps, figures, tables, and visual elements are correctly used to support discussion; writing is grammatically correct, fluent, concise, easy to read and understand, and uses appropriate word choice; references are well-structured and appropriate, supporting the report’s motivations.
criteria.reasoning: All required sections present, abstract approximately 155 words as specified. Three visual elements (a labelled decision flowchart and two tables) are integrated and referenced in text. Prose is concise and fluent, IEEE referencing is consistent and complete with access dates. Minor weakness: heading 'The Most Ethical Path' is more rhetorical than the rest.

evidence.quote: This report examines the dilemma of a quality assurance engineer, Rachel, who must decide whether to release servers

requirements.where: How should Rachel decide when to ship?

technical_issues.issue: 'Product engineers and later international customers' are bundled into a single stakeholder row with two unrelated interests, blurring who holds what stake.

Step 2 asks only whether the worst credible consequence is tolerable, whereas the text weights severity and likelihood; the likelihood branch is handled in step 1, but the flowchart reads as severity-only.
Attributing 'at least 81 of 236' trusts to the National Audit Office is broadly right but the phrasing merges the affected-trust count with the total; sourcing per claim would be tighter.

overall: An outstanding submission: sharply framed ethical issues, genuinely balanced argument, a reusable decision rule, and well-chosen quantitative case evidence. Minor imprecision in one stakeholder row and in Figure 1's severity/likelihood logic, but these do not undermine the analysis or conclusion.

feedback.summary: You produced an excellent report. You framed three distinct ethical issues, weighed arguments for and against shipping fairly, and built a reusable decision rule that carries through to your recommendation. Your quantitative case evidence is well chosen and your structure supports your conclusion. The remaining improvements are precision points in Table 1, Figure 1 and one sourcing detail.
next_steps: In Table 1, separate product engineers and international customers into distinct stakeholder rows so each group's interests and decision authority are clear.
Revise Figure 1 so step 2 explicitly weighs severity and likelihood, matching the text, rather than reading as severity-only.
Attribute each statistic to its own source, separating the count of affected trusts from the total number of trusts, for example in the 'Arguments against shipping' section.

criteria.C1: You identified three distinct ethical issues: calendar-driven test coverage, data loss misclassified as harmless, and a conflict of interest. You tied each to engineering design and organisational decision rights. Table 1 maps six stakeholder groups, including patients who cannot consent, with their interests and decision authority. This is a strong demonstration of context and stakeholder understanding.
criteria.C2: Your balanced discussion stands out because you state each pro-shipping argument fairly and then rebut it on its own terms, rather than simply opposing it. Table 2 shows who carries the risk under each option. Your conclusions are directed at several stakeholders, including Rachel, management, the health department and the chip supplier.
criteria.C3: Your report is structured so that each section builds towards the conclusion: issues, stakeholder map, arguments, decision rule, option comparison, then recommendation. Your conclusion restates the measured, reduced, accepted criterion established in the body, so it is well supported. The logic is easy to follow throughout.
criteria.C4: You substantiated your arguments with eight relevant sources, including a primary standard, a professional code and four external cases. Quantitative evidence such as the $475m charge, the $4.3bn figure and the 19,000 cancelled appointments is paired with qualitative reasoning from the Code of Ethics. You also acknowledged where the WannaCry analogy is imperfect, which shows a balanced understanding.
criteria.C5: Your report is fluently written, with appropriate sections, three integrated visual elements referenced in the text, and consistent, complete IEEE referencing. The prose is concise and easy to follow. One small refinement would be to make the heading 'The Most Ethical Path' more measured, to match the tone of the other headings.
